claim: Cessationists believe God no longer performs miracles.
quote: I believe God still heals and does miraculous things today
author: Thomas R. Schreiner
reference: Why I Am a Cessationist, “Miracles and Healings”
title: Miracles and the gift of miracles
response: Schreiner affirms present-day miracles while questioning whether individuals possess the New Testament gifts of healing and miracles. A claim about the continuation of a gift is different from a claim that God never acts miraculously.
context: He doubts that these gifts are present in churches today, calls for verification of healing claims, and allows for extraordinary signs in missionary settings. These qualifications describe his position; they should not be assigned to every cessationist.

criticism.author: R. T. Kendall
criticism.quote: the view that miracles “ceased” long ago and there is no hope for signs and wonders since we have the Bible
criticism.reference: RT’s New Year Letter, “Two things will change,” second change
criticism.edition: New Year’s Letter 2013, RT Kendall Ministries
criticism.context: This parenthetical defines cessationism in Kendall’s prediction of a coming spiritual awakening. Schreiner’s explicit affirmation of present miracles qualifies that broad description; it does not establish what every cessationist believes.

confessions.quote: yet is free to work without, above, and against them, at his pleasure.
confessions.edition: Historic English text as published by the Orthodox Presbyterian Church
confessions.context: “Them” refers to ordinary means. This affirms extraordinary providence; it neither promises particular miracles nor establishes continuing gifts of miracle-working.

confessions.quote: yet is free to work without, above, and against them at His pleasure.
confessions.edition: English text as published by Reformed Baptist Seminary; reference gives chapter and paragraph
confessions.context: The Baptist confession likewise affirms God’s freedom beyond ordinary means. This supports openness to extraordinary divine action without deciding whether particular miraculous gifts continue.

supporting_quotes.author: John MacArthur
supporting_quotes.quote: Now may I quickly say, God is still doing miracles today?
supporting_quotes.reference: The Gifts of the Body, Part 3, discussion following the purpose of authenticating miracles
supporting_quotes.edition: Grace to You sermon transcript, February 7, 1971; sermon 1313
supporting_quotes.context: MacArthur immediately distinguishes these miracles from signs authenticating new revelation. He attributes present miracles to God’s sovereign purpose and answers to faith and prayer, apart from a person’s miraculous gift. This affirmation does not endorse contemporary claims to possess the apostolic sign gifts.

claim: Cessationists are unlikely to believe God heals supernaturally today.
quote: Still, I pray for the healing of the sick and believe God can do so miraculously.
author: Thomas R. Schreiner
reference: It All Depends Upon Prophecy: A Brief Case for Nuanced Cessationism, opening discussion
title: Praying for what God can do
response: Schreiner explicitly prays for miraculous healing. His stated belief and practice provide a direct counterexample to Kendall’s broad expectation about cessationists’ disbelief in supernatural healing.
context: He regards miracles as relatively rare and distinguishes them from a gift regularly exercised by believers. He calls his position nuanced cessationism and allows for exceptional missionary situations. This is neither a promise that every prayer will result in healing nor a survey of all cessationist views.

criticism.author: R. T. Kendall
criticism.quote: You will not likely convince a cessationist to believe that the living God heals supernaturally today.
criticism.reference: Theology and worship, paragraph beginning “You will not likely convince”
criticism.edition: RT Kendall Ministries, online article; no publication date displayed
criticism.context: Kendall criticizes both charismatic excesses and conservative evangelical cessationism, while describing cessationists as good people rather than heretics. This sentence concerns belief in supernatural healing, not a claim that cessationists never pray for the sick.

confessions.quote: Prayer is to be made for things lawful;
confessions.edition: Historic English text as published by the Orthodox Presbyterian Church
confessions.context: This general rule permits lawful petitions, including healing. It does not specifically command miraculous healing or guarantee that the sick will recover.

supporting_quotes.author: OPC Committee on the Baptism and Gifts of the Holy Spirit
supporting_quotes.quote: the sovereign power of God to heal the sick, particularly in response to prayer, is a reality experienced
supporting_quotes.reference: Report of the Committee on the Baptism and Gifts of the Holy Spirit, V. Gifts of Healing in the Church
supporting_quotes.edition: Report presented to the Forty-fifth General Assembly of the Orthodox Presbyterian Church, 1978
supporting_quotes.context: The report distinguishes apostolic healing gifts from God’s continuing power to heal in response to prayer. It goes on to call this an expectation throughout church history. The committee was chaired by Richard B. Gaffin, Jr.; the assembly received the report for study. It is a committee report, not a constitutional confession or an individual statement by Gaffin.

claim: The gifts of the Spirit are unavailable today.
quote: It is the same Spirit who gives both temporary and continuing gifts to the church.
author: Sinclair B. Ferguson
reference: The Holy Spirit’s Ministry, paragraph beginning “What does this mean?”
edition: Ligonier Ministries, August 6, 2018; excerpt from The Holy Spirit
title: Some gifts cease; the Spirit keeps giving
response: Ferguson explicitly distinguishes temporary gifts from gifts that continue. His argument concerns particular gifts, rather than the withdrawal of every spiritual gift from the church.
context: Ferguson identifies miracle-working, revelatory prophecy, and tongues as temporary, while affirming continuing gifts and illumination. Kendall’s surrounding focus is miraculous gifts, so the dispute should not be inflated into a claim that he denies cessationists affirm any gifts at all. The precise scope of “gifts” matters.

criticism.author: RT Kendall Ministries (published teaching notes)
criticism.quote: In a word: the gifts of the Spirit are unavailable today
criticism.reference: The Gifts and the Fruit of the Holy Spirit, Introduction B.3.b.(2), p. 2
criticism.edition: Friday Night School of Theology notes hosted by RT Kendall Ministries; undated PDF
criticism.context: These unbylined notes, published on Kendall’s ministry website, discuss cessationism alongside signs and wonders and distinguish gifts from fruit. The surrounding focus on miraculous gifts matters: this wording must not be inflated into a denial that cessationists affirm teaching, service, or every other continuing gift.

confessions.quote: they have communion in each other’s gifts and graces,
confessions.edition: Historic English text as published by the Orthodox Presbyterian Church
confessions.context: Believers share gifts for mutual good. This affirms continuing gifted service without identifying whether prophecy, tongues, or healing belong among those gifts.

supporting_quotes.author: John MacArthur
supporting_quotes.quote: We said there are two categories of gifts: permanent and temporary.
supporting_quotes.reference: The Gifts of the Body, Part 3, opening distinction between permanent and temporary gifts
supporting_quotes.edition: Grace to You sermon transcript, February 7, 1971; sermon 1313
supporting_quotes.context: MacArthur explains that permanent gifts continue to build up the church, while temporary gifts confirmed the apostles’ and prophets’ message. This is an explicit distinction within spiritual gifts, not a rejection of all gifts. It does not resolve the disagreement over which gifts continue.

quote: We do not assert that God's Spirit is no longer actively working in dynamic and dramatic ways. We earnestly believe that he is.
author: Richard B. Gaffin, Jr.
reference: What about Prophecy and Tongues Today?, second paragraph
title: The Spirit’s present power
response: Gaffin’s affirmation establishes that he believes in the Spirit’s active power today. It answers a blanket description of cessationism as denying the Spirit’s work, but it does not by itself refute Kendall’s criticism that cessationism hinders particular activities of the Spirit.
context: Gaffin points to conversion and continuing gifts while denying foundational apostles and revelatory prophecy. Kendall argues that the disputed gifts remain available. Deciding whether cessationism quenches the Spirit requires addressing that biblical disagreement; quoting an affirmation of the Spirit alone is not enough.

criticism.author: R. T. Kendall
criticism.quote: without any question quenched the Holy Spirit Himself in the process.
criticism.reference: Holy Fire, paragraph beginning “There are two chapters”
criticism.edition: RT Kendall Ministries, article introducing the book Holy Fire; no publication date displayed
criticism.context: Kendall argues that making cessationism a dogma quenches the Spirit, while affirming cessationists’ Christian character and commitment to Scripture. This is a criticism of the position’s effects, not a statement that cessationists consciously deny all the Spirit’s activity.

confessions.quote: the inward illumination of the Spirit of God to be necessary for the saving understanding
confessions.edition: Historic English text as published by the Orthodox Presbyterian Church
confessions.context: The object of this understanding is Scripture. Continuing illumination is explicitly affirmed; this does not settle whether rejecting particular gifts quenches the Spirit.

claim: Fear is a major factor in adherence to cessationism.
quote: the fruit of the Spirit transforming us into the likeness of the character of Christ.
author: Sinclair B. Ferguson
reference: How does the modern church often misunderstand the Holy Spirit?, final answer paragraph
edition: Ask Ligonier transcript, lightly edited by the publisher for readability
title: Beliefs and motives are different questions
response: Ferguson gives a positive account of the Spirit’s transforming work. That helps describe what he affirms, but it cannot prove or disprove Storms’s claim about why some Christians remain cessationists. A person’s motives require evidence beyond their doctrinal label.
context: Storms names several factors rather than reducing every cessationist’s motives to fear. Ferguson’s answer here addresses Christian character, not the psychology of the debate. Read these as different kinds of statements; neither excerpt settles the prevalence of fear among cessationists.

criticism.author: Sam Storms
criticism.quote: I also think fear is a huge factor.
criticism.reference: Pneuma Review Interview with Sam Storms on Speaking in Tongues, answer to why Christians still adhere to cessationism
criticism.edition: Enjoying God Ministries, August 8, 2019; interview answers by Sam Storms
criticism.context: Storms also discusses inherited teaching, concern about abusive charismatic practices, and biblical texts cessationists understand differently. He offers several explanations; he does not say every cessationist is motivated only by fear.

claim: Cessationism cannot be robustly established from the Bible alone.
quote: The foundation for the church has been laid once-for-all
author: Thomas R. Schreiner
reference: The Miraculous Gifts and the Question of Cessationism, “Redemptive History”
edition: The Gospel Coalition, online theological essay
title: An argument about the church’s foundation
response: Schreiner offers an argument from the church’s apostolic and prophetic foundation, especially Ephesians 2:20. This identifies a biblical rationale that readers can evaluate. Merely citing the rationale does not establish that it is exegetically sound or answer Brown’s judgment that cessationist arguments fail.
context: Schreiner connects the foundation with apostolic revelation and the completed canon. Brown disputes the case by appealing to passages he understands to promise continuing gifts. This is an interpretive disagreement, not automatically a misrepresentation. Readers need to examine both arguments in their full sources.

criticism.author: Michael Brown
criticism.quote: I believe it is impossible to make an exegetically robust argument for cessationism using the Bible alone.
criticism.reference: Let the Reformed of the Lord Say No to Cessationism, paragraph beginning “Of course, each of these concepts”
criticism.context: Brown makes this judgment after arguing from John 14, Acts 2, 1 Corinthians, and James 5. This is a substantive challenge to cessationist exegesis, not itself a misquotation or a claim that cessationists never attempt biblical arguments.

confessions.quote: those former ways of God’s revealing his will unto his people being now ceased.
confessions.edition: Historic English text as published by the Orthodox Presbyterian Church
confessions.context: The context is committing revelation to writing. This explicitly affirms cessation of former revelatory ways, without enumerating every disputed gift or proving its biblical case.

claim: You don’t believe God still speaks to us.
title: God speaks through his living Word
quote: Does this mean God has stopped speaking? Certainly not, but He speaks today through His Word.
author: John MacArthur
reference: False Prophets and Lying Wonders, concluding paragraph
edition: Grace to You, January 11, 2010; article B100111
response: MacArthur explicitly denies that God has stopped speaking. He identifies Scripture as God’s present speech to his people. Reading, hearing, and faithfully preaching that Word are therefore occasions to hear God address us, rather than merely to learn what he once said to someone else.
context: Alvarez’s article contrasts atheists, deists, and cessationists using deliberately broad descriptions. Later she focuses on the most strident cessationists and on claims of God speaking personally. MacArthur really does reject fresh messages beyond Scripture; his affirmation should not be used to suggest that he accepts contemporary prophecy. The distinction is between the Spirit speaking through and applying the written Word and receiving additional revealed words. Cessationists differ about impressions and how to describe providential guidance. This entry concerns present divine speech; the separate prophecy entry concerns the continuation of revelatory gifts.

criticism.author: Carla Alvarez
criticism.quote: There is a God and he came to save us, but he doesn’t bother with us anymore. He doesn’t speak to us.
criticism.reference: Atheists, Cessationists, and What They Have in Common, comparison beginning “Cessationists”
criticism.kind: A broad description that needs qualification
criticism.context: Alvarez puts this sentence in her description of what cessationists believe; it is not her own denial that God speaks. The surrounding article argues for God’s personal involvement and later singles out the most strident cessationists. Her independent article is one published example of the accusation, not a statement representing every continuationist.

supporting_quotes.author: R. Fowler White
supporting_quotes.quote: In the Bible the church hears God’s true voice;
supporting_quotes.reference: Does God Speak Today Apart from the Bible?, concluding paragraph
supporting_quotes.edition: Chapter 4 in The Coming Evangelical Crisis, edited by John H. Armstrong (Moody Press, 1996); authorized reproduction at The Highway
supporting_quotes.context: White affirms that the Spirit presently speaks in Scripture and distinguishes illumination, leading, and conviction from new revelation. He disputes the claim that believers should expect additional revealed words outside Scripture.

confessions.quote: the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture.
confessions.edition: Historic English text as published by the Orthodox Presbyterian Church
confessions.context: The paragraph identifies the supreme judge of religious controversies. Its present description of the Spirit speaking in Scripture supports the distinction between a completed written revelation and God’s continuing address through it.

confessions.quote: The Spirit of God maketh the reading, but especially the preaching of the word, an effectual means
confessions.edition: Historic English text as published by the Orthodox Presbyterian Church
confessions.context: The answer goes on to describe enlightening, conviction, conversion, conformity to Christ, holiness, and comfort. It affirms the Spirit’s active use of the Word in hearers today, rather than treating Scripture as a dead record.

scriptures.reference: Hebrews 3:7–8 · “the Holy Ghost saith” in the words of a psalm
